title: Where Do New Cells Come From?

scenes.visual: Title card 'Where Do New Cells Come From?' over two cartoon cells side by side. Same world and colour map as the first film: warm cream background, flat cartoon shapes, no molecular structures; GOLD = light-microscope icon and limit; dark-BLUE cell outlines. New for this film: PLANT TISSUE panel tinted GREEN, ANIMAL TISSUE panel tinted PINK; FLUID MODEL = TEAL droplets and TEAL labels; DIVISION MODEL = ORANGE arrows and ORANGE labels; a LABEL top left reads 'many plant and animal tissues compared (examples)', with no count; a CELL COUNTER top right counts cells. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Idea three says every cell comes from a cell. The first scientists to argue for cells everywhere did not think so. So where did they think new cells came from? By the eighteen thirties, improved microscopes were in use. The argument was not only about seeing.
scenes.visual: The six-idea list from the lesson appears with idea 3, 'all cells arise from pre-existing cells', glowing ORANGE. A big question appears: 'where do new cells come from?'. A GOLD microscope icon with the label '1830s: improved microscopes' slides in at the side.
scenes.caption: Idea three says every cell comes from a cell. The first scientists to argue for cells everywhere did not think so. So where did they think new cells came from? By the 1830s, improved microscopes were in use. The argument was not only about seeing.
scenes.narration: Idea three says every cell comes from a cell. The first scientists to argue for cells everywhere did not think so. So where did they think new cells came from? By the 1830s, improved microscopes were in use. The argument was not only about seeing.

scenes.tts: In eighteen thirty-eight, Matthias Schleiden described plant tissues as made of cells. In eighteen thirty-nine, Theodor Schwann compared plant and animal tissues, such as tadpole cartilage. He found the same cellular plan.
scenes.visual: Two panels fill up. Left, GREEN, '1838 Schleiden: plant tissue', rows of dark-BLUE cell outlines. Right, PINK, '1839 Schwann: tadpole cartilage', rounded dark-BLUE cell outlines in a pale matrix. The same simple cell outline glows in both panels at once. More small GREEN and PINK panels stack behind them without any number, under the label 'many plant and animal tissues compared (examples)'.
scenes.caption: In 1838, Matthias Schleiden described plant tissues as made of cells. In 1839, Theodor Schwann compared plant and animal tissues, such as tadpole cartilage. He found the same cellular plan.
scenes.narration: In 1838, Matthias Schleiden described plant tissues as made of cells. In 1839, Theodor Schwann compared plant and animal tissues, such as tadpole cartilage. He found the same cellular plan.

scenes.tts: Comparison was the key step. Many kinds of tissue, plant and animal, showed one shared plan. That was evidence that plants and animals alike are built of cells.
scenes.visual: The GOLD microscope icon dims; a large '=' sign appears between the GREEN and PINK panels. Label: 'comparison was the key step'. The shared cell outline lifts out of both panels and merges into one outline in the centre, tagged 'one shared plan'.
scenes.narration: Comparison was the key step. Many kinds of tissue, plant and animal, showed one shared plan. That was evidence that plants and animals alike are built of cells.

scenes.tts: But Schleiden and Schwann also thought new cells could form inside a structureless fluid. Picture a crystal growing in a solution. No cell divides to make it. Schleiden proposed this for plants. Schwann extended it to animals.
scenes.visual: A pool of clear TEAL fluid, labelled 'structureless fluid'. Small TEAL specks gather and harden into a new cell outline, like a crystal growing; no cell divides to make it. Do NOT place the pool in a gap between cells: the lesson does not say where in the tissue the fluid was. A small GREEN leaf tag and a PINK tadpole tag sit beside it. Label in TEAL: 'fluid idea (Schleiden for plants, Schwann for animals): historical, wrong'.
scenes.narration: But Schleiden and Schwann also thought new cells could form inside a structureless fluid. Picture a crystal growing in a solution. No cell divides to make it. Schleiden proposed this for plants. Schwann extended it to animals.

scenes.tts: So there were two models. In the fluid model, a new cell forms inside a structureless fluid, and no cell divides. In the division model, one existing cell splits into two.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left, TEAL heading 'fluid model': a new outline condenses from TEAL specks inside a TEAL pool, no cell dividing. Right, ORANGE heading 'division model': one dark-BLUE cell stretches, a waist forms, and it splits into two, ORANGE arrows showing parent to daughters. Both loops repeat slowly, labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: So there were two models. In the fluid model, a new cell forms inside a structureless fluid, and no cell divides. In the division model, one existing cell splits into two.

scenes.tts: Suppose you could watch a growing tissue for a while. What would each model lead you to expect to find?
scenes.visual: A blank growing-tissue panel with a few cells and empty spaces. Two empty answer boxes below it, one TEAL 'if fluid model:', one ORANGE 'if division model:'. A question mark pulses.
scenes.narration: Suppose you could watch a growing tissue for a while. What would each model lead you to expect to find?

scenes.visual: Hold on the two empty answer boxes with a 5-second countdown ring.

scenes.tts: The fluid model predicts new cells taking shape out of fluid, with no cell dividing. The division model predicts a series of stages. One cell pinches in two, then its daughters split again. Watching over time can tell the two models apart.
scenes.visual: The TEAL box fills: an outline condenses out of a TEAL pool, tagged 'no cell divided'. The ORANGE box fills: a series of frames, one cell with a pinched waist, then two daughters, then four, tagged 'a series of stages'; the CELL COUNTER top right steps 1, 2, 4 (schematic). A small clock icon labelled 'over time' sits between the boxes.
scenes.narration: The fluid model predicts new cells taking shape out of fluid, with no cell dividing. The division model predicts a series of stages. One cell pinches in two, then its daughters split again. Watching over time can tell the two models apart.

scenes.tts: In eighteen fifty-two, Robert Remak published evidence that new cells form when existing cells divide. In eighteen fifty-five, Rudolf Virchow spread the idea widely in a short article. Every cell comes from a cell. Remak's evidence came first; Virchow made it widely known.
scenes.visual: A timeline strip slides in: '1852 Remak: new cells form by division' with an ORANGE dividing-cell icon, then '1855 Virchow: every cell comes from a cell' written large in ORANGE. The ORANGE division panel grows to fill the screen.
scenes.caption: In 1852, Robert Remak published evidence that new cells form when existing cells divide. In 1855, Rudolf Virchow spread the idea widely in a short article. Every cell comes from a cell. Remak's evidence came first; Virchow made it widely known.
scenes.narration: In 1852, Robert Remak published evidence that new cells form when existing cells divide. In 1855, Rudolf Virchow spread the idea widely in a short article. Every cell comes from a cell. Remak's evidence came first; Virchow made it widely known.

scenes.tts: The fluid idea was wrong, so it was dropped. The core stayed: plants and animals are made of cells. A corrected idea took the fluid idea's place: cells come from existing cells.
scenes.visual: The TEAL fluid-model panel gets a red diagonal line through it and slides off screen. The central 'one shared plan' outline from earlier stays, glowing, labelled 'core kept'. Then the ORANGE 'every cell comes from a cell' slides into the space the TEAL panel left, tagged 'corrected idea, replacing the fluid idea'. Heading: 'the cell theory, corrected'.
scenes.narration: The fluid idea was wrong, so it was dropped. The core stayed: plants and animals are made of cells. A corrected idea took the fluid idea's place: cells come from existing cells.

scenes.tts: That is how a scientific theory works. It is a well-tested explanation, tied to many lines of evidence. When strong new evidence appears, it can be revised. Being revised does not make it a guess.
scenes.visual: A box labelled 'scientific theory' with three arrows pointing into it from small icons: 'plant tissues', 'animal tissues', 'cells dividing'. A small eraser removes the TEAL fluid tag from the box. A crossed-out speech bubble reads 'just a guess'.
scenes.narration: That is how a scientific theory works. It is a well-tested explanation, tied to many lines of evidence. When strong new evidence appears, it can be revised. Being revised does not make it a guess.

scenes.tts: One limit on the rule. Every cell comes from a cell is about cells living today. How the very first cells arose is a separate question that scientists still study.
scenes.visual: The ORANGE line 'every cell comes from a cell' with a tag 'cells living today'. Far off to one side, a faint, separate question mark labelled 'the very first cells: a separate question'.
scenes.narration: One limit on the rule. Every cell comes from a cell is about cells living today. How the very first cells arose is a separate question that scientists still study.

scenes.visual: End card: the Hex mascot beside the line 'A theory keeps what evidence supports and drops what it does not.' A small TEAL tag is crossed out and an ORANGE arrow kept beneath the text.
